\begin{definition}\label{def:1.7}
(Spaces, duals, and pairing.)
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space endowed with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
Let \(E^{*}\) be the dual space of linear functionals on \(E\).
For \(s\in E^{*}\) and \(x\in E\), denote by \(\langle s,x\rangle\) the value of \(s\) at \(x\).
When an inner product is used, it is denoted by the same bracket notation, with an index when necessary.
\end{definition}

Proposition 1.1.1
proof:
\begin{proof}\label{proof:prop:1.2}
If \(u=0\), then \(A^{*}u=0\) and \eqref{eq:1.2} is trivial.
Assume \(u\ne 0\) and set \(\bar u = u/\|u\|_2\), so \(\|\bar u\|_2=1\).
By the dual-norm definition \eqref{eq:dual_norm_def} and the adjoint identity \eqref{eq:adjoint_def}, we have
\[
\|A^{*}u\|_{1,*}
=\max_{\|x\|_1=1}\langle A^{*}u,x\rangle_1
=\max_{\|x\|_1=1}\langle Ax,u\rangle_2
=\|u\|_2\max_{\|x\|_1=1}\langle Ax,\bar u\rangle_2.
\]
Since \(\|\bar u\|_2=1\), for every \(x\) with \(\|x\|_1=1\) we have
\(\langle Ax,\bar u\rangle_2\le \max_{\|v\|_2=1}\langle Ax,v\rangle_2\).
Taking the maximum over \(\|x\|_1=1\) yields
\[
\max_{\|x\|_1=1}\langle Ax,\bar u\rangle_2
\le \max_{\|x\|_1=1,\ \|v\|_2=1}\langle Ax,v\rangle_2
=\|A\|_{1,2}
\]
by \eqref{eq:operator_norm_def}. Combining the displays gives
\(\|A^{*}u\|_{1,*}\le \|u\|_2\,\|A\|_{1,2}\), i.e. \eqref{eq:1.2}.
\end{proof}

Proposition 1.2.1
proof:
\begin{proof}\label{proof:prop:ex1}
We follow the computations shown in Example~1 of the paper.

Let \(t\in\mathbb{R}^m\) be the vector with components \(t^{(j)}=\langle a_j,x\rangle_1-b^{(j)}\).
A standard (and directly checkable) identity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ex1:l1_duality}
\max_{1\le j\le m}|t^{(j)}|\;=\;\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m s^{(j)}t^{(j)}:\ \sum_{j=1}^m|s^{(j)}|\le 1\right\}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for any \(s\) with \(\sum|s^{(j)}|\le 1\) we have
\(\sum s^{(j)}t^{(j)}\le \sum |s^{(j)}|\,\max_i|t^{(i)}|\le \max_i|t^{(i)}|\),
so the right-hand side is \(\le\max_i|t^{(i)}|\). Equality is attained by taking \(s\) supported on an index \(j\) achieving the maximum, with sign matching \(t^{(j)}\).

(2) Applying \eqref{eq:ex1:l1_duality} with \(t^{(j)}=\langle a_j,x\rangle_1-b^{(j)}\) gives
\(
 f(x)=\max_{\sum|u^{(j)}|\le 1}\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}(\langle a_j,x\rangle_1-b^{(j)})
\),
which is exactly \eqref{eq:ex1:Rm_representation}. This is of the form \eqref{eq:2.2} with \(E_2=\mathbb{R}^m\), \(Q_2=\{u:\sum|u^{(j)}|\le 1\}\), \(\hat f\equiv 0\), and \(\hat\phi(u)=\langle b,u\rangle_2\).

(3) For simplex lifting, write each \(u^{(j)}\) as a difference of nonnegative parts:
\(u^{(j)}=u_1^{(j)}-u_2^{(j)}\) with \(u_1^{(j)},u_2^{(j)}\ge 0\).
Then \(\sum_{j=1}^m|u^{(j)}|\le 1\) is equivalent to the existence of such \((u_1,u_2)\) with
\(\sum_{j=1}^m(u_1^{(j)}+u_2^{(j)})=1\) (after possibly adding slack so the sum is exactly 1).
Substituting \(u=u_1-u_2\) into \eqref{eq:ex1:Rm_representation} yields \eqref{eq:ex1:simplex_representation}.

(1) For the conjugate-style representation, take \(A=I\) and define
\(\hat\phi(u)=\max_x\{\langle u,x\rangle_1-f(x)\}\).
Using \eqref{eq:ex1:l1_duality} to expand \(f(x)\) and then exchanging \(\max_x\) with \(\min_s\) exactly as carried out in the paper's displayed computation, one obtains the explicit form \eqref{eq:ex1:phi_hat_conjugate_like}.
This completes the construction of explicit max-structure representations.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 1.2.4
Proposition 1.2.2
proof:
\begin{proof}\label{proof:prop:2.4}
Fix any \(u\in Q_2\). For any \(t\in(0,1)\), define \(u_t=(1-t)u_0+t u\). Since \(Q_2\) is convex, \(u_t\in Q_2\).
Because \(u_0\) minimizes \(d_2\) over \(Q_2\), we have
\(d_2(u_0)\le d_2(u_t)\).

By \(\sigma_2\)-strong convexity of \(d_2\) on \(Q_2\), for all \(v,w\in Q_2\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\) we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strong_convex_subgrad}
d_2((1-t)v+t w)\le (1-t)d_2(v)+t d_2(w)-\frac{\sigma_2}{2}\,t(1-t)\,\|w-v\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
Applying \eqref{eq:strong_convex_subgrad} with \(v=u_0\) and \(w=u\) gives
\[
 d_2(u_t)\le (1-t)d_2(u_0)+t d_2(u)-\frac{\sigma_2}{2}\,t(1-t)\,\|u-u_0\|_2^2.
\]
Combining this with \(d_2(u_0)\le d_2(u_t)\) yields
\[
 d_2(u_0)\le (1-t)d_2(u_0)+t d_2(u)-\frac{\sigma_2}{2}\,t(1-t)\,\|u-u_0\|_2^2.
\]
Rearranging and dividing by \(t>0\) gives
\[
 d_2(u)\ge d_2(u_0)+\frac{\sigma_2}{2}(1-t)\,\|u-u_0\|_2^2.
\]
Since this holds for all \(t\in(0,1)\), letting \(t\to 0^{+}\) gives
\(d_2(u)\ge d_2(u_0)+\frac{\sigma_2}{2}\|u-u_0\|_2^2\).
Using the normalization \(d_2(u_0)=0\) yields \eqref{eq:2.4}.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 1.2.5
Theorem 1.2.1
Proposition 1.2.3
proof:
\begin{proof}\label{proof:prop:2.7}
Fix any \(x\in E_1\).

(First inequality \(f_\mu(x)\le f_0(x)\).)
For every \(u\in Q_2\), we have
\(\langle Ax,u\rangle_2-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)\le \langle Ax,u\rangle_2-\hat\phi(u)\)
because \(\mu>0\) and \(d_2(u)\ge 0\) (after normalization at the prox-center, the minimum value is \(0\), so all values are nonnegative).
Taking the maximum over \(u\in Q_2\) gives
\(f_\mu(x)\le f_0(x)\).

(Second inequality \(f_0(x)\le f_\mu(x)+\mu D_2\).)
By definition of \(D_2\) in \eqref{eq:D2_def}, for every \(u\in Q_2\) we have \(d_2(u)\le D_2\), hence
\[
\langle Ax,u\rangle_2-\hat\phi(u)
\le \langle Ax,u\rangle_2-\hat\phi(u)-\mu d_2(u)+\mu D_2.
\]
Taking the maximum over \(u\in Q_2\) on the left yields \(f_0(x)\), and on the right yields \(f_\mu(x)+\mu D_2\). Therefore
\(f_0(x)\le f_\mu(x)+\mu D_2\).

Combining both inequalities proves \eqref{eq:2.7}.
\end{proof}

proof:
\begin{proof}\label{proof:prop:4.17}
The minimax identity follows from the bilinearity of $\langle B(v),w-v\rangle_1$ in the variables $(w,v)$ and convexity/compactness of $Q$.
Expanding $\langle B(v),w-v\rangle_1=\langle \mathcal{B}v+b,w\rangle_1-\langle \mathcal{B}v+b,v\rangle_1$ shows that the term $\langle \mathcal{B}x,x\rangle_1$ becomes part of the smooth component $\hat f$ in the dual variant, while the max-part uses $\hat\phi(u)=\langle b,u\rangle_1$.
The oracle formula for $f_\mu$ follows by applying the smoothing definition \eqref{eq:2.5}.

Since $\hat f(x)=\langle b,x\rangle_1+\langle \mathcal{B}x,x\rangle_1$ has gradient Lipschitz constant $\|\mathcal{B}\|_{1,2}$, we have $M=\|\mathcal{B}\|_{1,2}$ in Theorem~3.
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:4.4} yields the stated bound with an additional $\sqrt{MD_1/(\sigma_1\varepsilon)}$ term compared to \eqref{eq:4.21}.
\end{proof}
